knowledge_answers.rationale: A called Wide does not count as one of the over.
An over requires six valid balls; neither the No ball nor the Wide is valid, leaving four valid balls.
A deliberate-short finding invokes the special rule rather than ordinary short-run scoring; all batting-side runs are disallowed and five Penalty runs go to the fielding side.

Hit wicket is limited to specified phases tied to receiving or immediately setting off; ordinary running after those actions is an express not-out situation; merely breaking the wicket then does not automatically create another dismissal.

No ball prevents Stumped; the special Run-out exception protects a striker out of ground, not attempting a run, when the keeper alone puts down the wicket after No ball; with both candidate routes barred, there is no dismissal.
